title: The spectral theorem proved
objectives: Prove the spectral theorem for symmetric matrices without notes.

screens.title: One direction, one plane
screens.prose: Take $\mathbf{A} = \begin{pmatrix}2&1&1\\1&2&1\\1&1&2\end{pmatrix}$, a real symmetric matrix. The canvas draws $\mathbf{q} = (1, 1, 1)$ and the plane $U$ of vectors with $u_1 + u_2 + u_3 = 0$. Rotate it to see that $\mathbf{q}$ is perpendicular to $U$.
screens.question: $\mathbf{A}(1, 1, 1) = \lambda(1, 1, 1)$. What is $\lambda$?

hints.text: Each entry of $\mathbf{A}(1, 1, 1)$ is a row sum.

feedback.correct: Right. Each row sums to $2 + 1 + 1 = 4$, so $\mathbf{A}(1, 1, 1) = (4, 4, 4)$.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Each entry of $\mathbf{A}(1, 1, 1)$ is a row sum of $\mathbf{A}$.

byKey.one: 1 is the other eigenvalue of $\mathbf{A}$. For $(1, 1, 1)$ each entry is a row sum, $2 + 1 + 1 = 4$.
byKey.twelve: You added all nine entries. Each entry of $\mathbf{A}(1, 1, 1)$ is one row sum, 4.

explain.text: $\mathbf{A}(1, 1, 1) = (4, 4, 4)$, so $(1, 1, 1)$ is an eigenvector for 4. The plane $U$ is its orthogonal complement. Next we ask what $\mathbf{A}$ does to $U$.

canvas.caption: $\mathbf{q}$ at 0.8 of its length; $\mathbf{A}\mathbf{q} = 4\mathbf{q}$ at 0.3 of its length.

screens.title: The plane stays put
screens.prose: Move the sliders to choose $\mathbf{u} = (a, b, -a - b)$ in $U$. The dashed arrow is $\mathbf{A}\mathbf{u}$. The caption adds up its entries.

derive.caption: $\mathbf{A}\mathbf{u}$ = ({{fixed(a, 1)}}, {{fixed(b, 1)}}, {{fixed(0 - a - b, 1)}}); its entries add to {{fixed(a + b + (0 - a - b), 1)}}

screens.question: Take $\mathbf{u} = (1, 2, -3)$. Fill in $\mathbf{A}\mathbf{u}$.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Row 1 of $\mathbf{A}$ dotted with $(1, 2, -3)$ is $2 + 2 - 3$.

byKey.nine: You kept only $2 \cdot (-3) = -6$ and dropped the other two terms of row 3. Row 3 gives $1 + 2 - 6 = -3$.

explain.text: $\mathbf{A}\mathbf{u} = \mathbf{u}$ for every $\mathbf{u}$ in $U$, so $\mathbf{A}$ maps $U$ into $U$. We say $U$ is **invariant** under $\mathbf{A}$. That the complement of an eigenvector is invariant is the heart of the proof.

screens.title: Eigenvectors inside the plane
screens.prose: So $\mathbf{A}$ acts on the invariant plane $U$ as the identity: every non-zero $\mathbf{u} \in U$ is an eigenvector for 1. The eigenvalues of $\mathbf{A}$ are 4, 1, 1. Pick two in $U$: $(1, -1, 0)$ and $(1, 0, -1)$.
screens.question: What is $\langle (1, -1, 0), (1, 0, -1) \rangle$?

hints.text: Multiply the first entries, then the second, then the third.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Multiply entry by entry and add.

byKey.zero: You expected 0, because the matrix is symmetric. Only eigenvectors for different eigenvalues must be perpendicular.
byKey.pairs: You paired the non-zero entries in turn, $1 \cdot 1 + (-1)(-1)$. Pair by position: $1 \cdot 1 + (-1) \cdot 0 + 0 \cdot (-1) = 1$.

explain.text: The inner product is 1, so these two eigenvectors for 1 meet at $60°$. Both lie in $U$, which is a whole eigenspace. We are free to choose a better pair inside it.

screens.title: Straighten the pair
screens.prose: Run Gram-Schmidt (level 3 l13) inside $U$. Take $\mathbf{q}_2 = \tfrac{1}{\sqrt2}(1, -1, 0)$. Then remove from $(1, 0, -1)$ its part along $\mathbf{q}_2$: $\mathbf{f} = (1, 0, -1) - \langle (1, 0, -1), \mathbf{q}_2 \rangle\mathbf{q}_2$.
screens.question: What is $\mathbf{f}$?

feedback.generic: Not quite right. $\langle (1, 0, -1), \mathbf{q}_2 \rangle = \tfrac{1}{\sqrt2}$, so the part along $\mathbf{q}_2$ is $\tfrac12(1, -1, 0)$.

byKey.full: You subtracted all of $(1, -1, 0)$. Only half of it lies along $\mathbf{q}_2$.

explain.text: $\mathbf{f} = (0.5, 0.5, -1)$, still in $U$ since $0.5 + 0.5 - 1 = 0$. So it is still an eigenvector for 1. Normalised, $\mathbf{q}_3 = \tfrac{1}{\sqrt6}(1, 1, -2)$.

screens.title: The orthonormal eigenbasis
screens.prose: $\mathbf{Q}$ has columns $\mathbf{q}_1 = \tfrac{1}{\sqrt3}(1, 1, 1)$, $\mathbf{q}_2 = \tfrac{1}{\sqrt2}(1, -1, 0)$ and $\mathbf{q}_3 = \tfrac{1}{\sqrt6}(1, 1, -2)$. The canvas draws them at equal scale: three perpendicular unit arrows. Then $\mathbf{Q}^T\mathbf{A}\mathbf{Q} = \boldsymbol{\Lambda}$ is diagonal.
screens.question: Fill in the diagonal of $\boldsymbol{\Lambda}$: the eigenvalue of each column.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. $\mathbf{q}_1$ is along $(1, 1, 1)$; $\mathbf{q}_2$ and $\mathbf{q}_3$ lie in $U$.

byKey.third: $\mathbf{q}_3$ lies in $U$, where $\mathbf{A}$ is the identity. Its eigenvalue is 1, not 0.

explain.text: Each column is a unit eigenvector, and they are pairwise perpendicular, so $\mathbf{Q}^T\mathbf{Q} = \mathbf{I}$. Then $\mathbf{Q}^T\mathbf{A}\mathbf{Q} = \operatorname{diag}(4, 1, 1)$. This is the spectral theorem for $\mathbf{A}$: $\mathbf{A} = \mathbf{Q}\boldsymbol{\Lambda}\mathbf{Q}^T$.

screens.title: Always orthogonal?
screens.prose: A classmate says eigenvectors of a symmetric matrix are always orthogonal. So she builds $\mathbf{Q}$ from $\mathbf{q}_1$, $\tfrac{1}{\sqrt2}(1, -1, 0)$ and $\tfrac{1}{\sqrt2}(1, 0, -1)$, three unit eigenvectors.
screens.question: Is her $\mathbf{Q}$ orthogonal, with $\mathbf{Q}^T\mathbf{Q} = \mathbf{I}$?

options.text: No: the last two columns have inner product $\tfrac12$
Yes: eigenvectors of a symmetric matrix are orthogonal
options.why: Only eigenvectors for different eigenvalues must be. These two share the eigenvalue 1, and their inner product is $\tfrac12$.
Unit length is half of orthonormal. The columns must also be pairwise perpendicular.

options.text: No: $\mathbf{q}_1$ is not perpendicular to the others
options.why: $\mathbf{q}_1$ is perpendicular to all of $U$. The trouble is the pair inside $U$.

hints.text: Both of the last two columns lie in $U$, the eigenspace for 1.
So the columns are not orthonormal.

feedback.correct: Right. Inside a repeated eigenspace you must choose an orthonormal basis.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Compute the inner product of the last two columns.

byKey.yes: You applied the rule to a repeated eigenvalue. Perpendicular is guaranteed only for distinct eigenvalues; inside $U$, Gram-Schmidt does the job.

explain.text: $\langle \tfrac{1}{\sqrt2}(1, -1, 0), \tfrac{1}{\sqrt2}(1, 0, -1) \rangle = \tfrac12$, so $\mathbf{Q}^T\mathbf{Q} \ne \mathbf{I}$. Eigenvectors for different eigenvalues are orthogonal by l16. Within one eigenspace, any basis will do, so we pick an orthonormal one.

screens.title: The real spectral theorem
screens.prose: Theorem (Axler 7.29). Let $\mathbf{A}$ be a real $n \times n$ matrix. It is symmetric exactly when $\mathbb{R}^n$ has an orthonormal basis of its eigenvectors. The proof needs a real unit eigenvector to start. As a complex matrix, $\mathbf{A}$ has an eigenvalue $\lambda$ (l15), and $\lambda$ is real (l16). In matrix form the theorem reads $$\mathbf{A} = \mathbf{Q}\boldsymbol{\Lambda}\mathbf{Q}^T, \quad \mathbf{Q}^T\mathbf{Q} = \mathbf{I}, \ \boldsymbol{\Lambda} \text{ diagonal}.$$
screens.question: Why does $\mathbf{A}$ then have a real eigenvector for $\lambda$?

options.text: $\mathbf{A} - \lambda\mathbf{I}$ is a real matrix of rank below $n$, so it has a non-zero real kernel vector
Every eigenvector of a real matrix is real
options.why: The rotation's eigenvector is $(i, 1)$. What helps here is that $\lambda$ is real.
Invertibility plays no part: the zero matrix is symmetric and has the real eigenvector $\mathbf{e}_1$.
Any real eigenvalue will do; size plays no part.

feedback.correct: Right. A real singular matrix has a non-zero real null vector, by rank-nullity.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. $\mathbf{A} - \lambda\mathbf{I}$ is real when $\lambda$ is real. What does its rank tell us?

explain.text: $\mathbf{A} - \lambda\mathbf{I}$ is real and not injective over $\mathbb{C}$, so its rank is below $n$. Elimination keeps a real matrix's rank the same over $\mathbb{R}$, so rank-nullity gives a real kernel vector. The complex version of the theorem concerns normal operators (Axler 7.31) and is not examined.

screens.title: The proof by induction
screens.prose: Prove the theorem by induction on $n$. Assume it for symmetric matrices of size $n - 1$. Each line carries its reason.
screens.question: Put the lines in order. One line does not belong: move it to Left out.

lines.text: For $n = 1$, $\mathbf{A} = (a)$ is diagonal and $(1)$ is an orthonormal eigenbasis.
For $n > 1$: $\mathbf{A}$ has a complex eigenvalue (l15), which is real since $\mathbf{A}$ is self-adjoint (l16).
$\mathbf{A} - \lambda\mathbf{I}$ is real with the same rank over $\mathbb{R}$ and $\mathbb{C}$, below $n$. So it has a real kernel vector; normalise it to $\mathbf{q}_1$.

$U$ is invariant: for $\mathbf{u} \in U$, $\langle \mathbf{A}\mathbf{u}, \mathbf{q}_1 \rangle = \langle \mathbf{u}, \mathbf{A}\mathbf{q}_1 \rangle = \lambda\langle \mathbf{u}, \mathbf{q}_1 \rangle = 0$, by symmetry.
$\mathbf{A}$ restricted to $U$ is self-adjoint for the inner product $U$ inherits.
Applied to $\mathbf{A}|_U$ in an orthonormal basis of $U$, the hypothesis gives an orthonormal eigenbasis $\mathbf{q}_2, \dots, \mathbf{q}_n$ of $U$.
$\mathbf{q}_1 \perp U$, so $\mathbf{q}_1, \dots, \mathbf{q}_n$ is an orthonormal eigenbasis of $\mathbb{R}^n$, and $\mathbf{A} = \mathbf{Q}\boldsymbol{\Lambda}\mathbf{Q}^T$.
$U$ is invariant because $\mathbf{A}$ is invertible, so $\mathbf{A}U$ has dimension $n - 1$.
lines.why: Invertibility gives the dimension of $\mathbf{A}U$, not that $\mathbf{A}U \subseteq U$. The step needs symmetry, and the zero matrix is not invertible.

hints.text: Then: real eigenvalue, $\mathbf{q}_1$, $\dim U$, invariance, restriction.
End with the hypothesis, assembling the basis, and the converse.

feedback.correct: Right. Base case, a real unit eigenvector, an invariant complement, induction, then the converse.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. After the base case, find $\mathbf{q}_1$, then its complement, then use the hypothesis.

byKey.x1: You used invertibility for invariance. The step needs $\langle \mathbf{A}\mathbf{u}, \mathbf{q}_1 \rangle = \langle \mathbf{u}, \mathbf{A}\mathbf{q}_1 \rangle$, which is symmetry.
byKey.left-out: You left out a line the proof needs.

explain.text: A real unit eigenvector $\mathbf{q}_1$ splits off, and symmetry keeps its complement $U$ invariant. On $U$ the restriction is self-adjoint and one size smaller, so induction finishes. The converse is one line of transposes.

screens.title: A reason for every line
screens.prose: Here is the skeleton again, without its reasons. Recall the reason each line needs. Two reasons are spare and fit no line.
screens.question: Drag each reason to its line.

tokens.text: l15 gives a complex eigenvalue; l16 makes it real
$\mathbf{A} - \lambda\mathbf{I}$ is real and singular, so its real kernel is not $\{\mathbf{0}\}$
the induction hypothesis, as $\mathbf{A}$ on $U$ is self-adjoint
every real polynomial has a real root

slots.label: There is a real unit eigenvector $\mathbf{q}_1$.

hints.text: Start with the line about invariance.
Invariance moves $\mathbf{A}$ across the inner product.
Two reasons, invertibility and real roots, are never used.

feedback.correct: Right. Every line of the proof has its reason.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Match each reason to the line it justifies; two reasons are not used.

byKey.x1: You used invertibility. No line of the proof needs it: the zero matrix is symmetric and singular.
byKey.x2: You used real roots of real polynomials. That is false ($z^2 + 1$), which is why the proof goes through $\mathbb{C}$.
byKey.t4: Symmetry is the reason for invariance, the step $\mathbf{A}U \subseteq U$.
byKey.t5: The induction hypothesis is what gives the orthonormal eigenbasis of $U$.

explain.text: The real eigenvalue comes from l15 and l16, and the real eigenvector from rank. Dimension comes from l14 and invariance from symmetry. The hypothesis finishes $U$, and transposing gives the converse.

screens.title: Find the flaw
screens.prose: A classmate runs the proof on $\mathbf{N} = \begin{pmatrix}2&1\\0&3\end{pmatrix}$, which is not symmetric. The lower canvas draws $(0, 1)$ and $\mathbf{N}(0, 1)$, with the band of $(0, 1)$.

rows: $\mathbf{N}$ has the real eigenvalue 2 with unit eigenvector $\mathbf{q}_1 = (1, 0)$.
So $(1, 0), (0, 1)$ is an orthonormal eigenbasis of $\mathbf{N}$. $\blacksquare$

screens.question: Tap the line that does not follow.

hints.text: It is $(1, 3)$, off the band of $(0, 1)$.
So the invariance line fails: it used symmetry that $\mathbf{N}$ lacks.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Test each line on $\mathbf{N}$ itself.

byKey.r1: Line 2 is true: the complement of $(1, 0)$ in $\mathbb{R}^2$ is the $y$-axis.
byKey.r3: Line 4 would follow from line 3. The fault is earlier.

explain.text: $\langle \mathbf{N}\mathbf{u}, \mathbf{q}_1 \rangle = \langle \mathbf{u}, \mathbf{N}\mathbf{q}_1 \rangle$ needs $\mathbf{N}^T = \mathbf{N}$. Here $\mathbf{N}(0, 1) = (1, 3)$, which has inner product 1 with $\mathbf{q}_1$. So $U$ is not invariant, and $(0, 1)$ is no eigenvector.

screens.title: The spectral theorem in NumPy
screens.prose: `spectral(A)` returns the eigenvalues in ascending order and $\mathbf{Q}$, whose columns are orthonormal eigenvectors. It must refuse a matrix that is not symmetric. The starter uses `np.linalg.eig`, which accepts any matrix and does not sort.
screens.question: Fix `spectral(A)`. Check `np.allclose(A, A.T)`, raise `ValueError` if it fails, then use `np.linalg.eigh`.

widget.starter:
import numpy as np

def spectral(A):
    A = np.array(A, dtype=float)
    w, Q = np.linalg.eig(A)
    return w, Q
widget.solution:
import numpy as np

def spectral(A):
    A = np.array(A, dtype=float)
    if not np.allclose(A, A.T):
        raise ValueError("A is not symmetric")
    w, Q = np.linalg.eigh(A)
    return w, Q

tests.setup: A = np.array([[2, 1, 1], [1, 2, 1], [1, 1, 2]], dtype=float); w, Q = spectral(A)

widget.how: Check runs 5 hidden tests. Three use the hook matrix: sorted eigenvalues, $\mathbf{Q}^T\mathbf{Q} = \mathbf{I}$ and $\mathbf{Q}\boldsymbol{\Lambda}\mathbf{Q}^T = \mathbf{A}$. Then the equicorrelated matrix with $\rho = 0.5$, and $\mathbf{N}$, which must raise. The first run loads NumPy, which takes a few seconds.

feedback.correct: Right. `eigh` assumes symmetry, so we check it first; it returns sorted eigenvalues and orthonormal columns.
feedback.generic: Some tests failed. Read the first failing row.

byKey.test-1: Your eigenvalues are not in ascending order. `np.linalg.eigh` sorts them; `eig` does not.
byKey.test-5: $\mathbf{N}$ is not symmetric and must raise `ValueError`. Test `np.allclose(A, A.T)` first.
byKey.error: Your code stopped with an error. Check that you return the pair `(w, Q)`.

explain.text:
`eigh` reads only one triangle of the matrix, so a non-symmetric input would be silently wrong. The check makes the hypothesis of the theorem explicit. Its output is the theorem's $\boldsymbol{\Lambda}$ and $\mathbf{Q}$.

```python
if not np.allclose(A, A.T):
    raise ValueError("A is not symmetric")
w, Q = np.linalg.eigh(A)
```

screens.title: Equicorrelated assets
screens.prose: Three assets each have correlation $\rho$ with the others. The correlation matrix has eigenvalues $1 + 2\rho$, for the market mode $(1, 1, 1)$, and $1 - \rho$ twice. Move $\rho$ and watch them. At $\rho = 0.5$ they are 2, 0.5 and 0.5.
screens.question: At $\rho = 0.5$, what is the variance of the equal-weight portfolio $\mathbf{w} = \tfrac13(1, 1, 1)$, in correlation units?

feedback.correct: Right. $\mathbf{w}$ lies on the market mode, so $\mathbf{w}^T\mathbf{C}\mathbf{w} = 2\|\mathbf{w}\|^2 = 2 \times \tfrac13 \approx 0.6667$.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. $\mathbf{w}$ is an eigenvector for 2, and $\|\mathbf{w}\|^2 = \tfrac13$.

byKey.lam: You used the eigenvalue alone. The variance is $\lambda\|\mathbf{w}\|^2$, and $\|\mathbf{w}\|^2 = \tfrac13$.
byKey.spread: You used $1 - \rho = 0.5$, giving $0.5 \times \tfrac13 \approx 0.1667$. The equal-weight portfolio is the market mode, with eigenvalue $1 + 2\rho = 2$.
byKey.ninth: You kept only the three diagonal 1s, $\tfrac39$. The off-diagonal terms add $6 \times 0.5$, so the sum is $\tfrac{6}{9}$.

explain.text: $\mathbf{w}^T\mathbf{C}\mathbf{w} = 2 \times \tfrac13 \approx 0.6667$, matching $\tfrac{3 + 6 \times 0.5}{9}$. At $\rho = -0.5$ the smallest eigenvalue is 0, the boundary. Below that it turns negative, so no correlation matrix has every off-diagonal entry $-0.6$.

ideas: A real $n \times n$ matrix is symmetric exactly when it has an orthonormal basis of eigenvectors: $\mathbf{A} = \mathbf{Q}\boldsymbol{\Lambda}\mathbf{Q}^T$.
The proof finds a real unit eigenvector $\mathbf{q}_1$, shows by symmetry that $\mathbf{q}_1^\perp$ is invariant, and applies induction there.
Only eigenvectors for distinct eigenvalues are automatically orthogonal. Inside a repeated eigenspace, choose an orthonormal basis by Gram-Schmidt.
summary.trap: Eigenvectors sharing an eigenvalue need not be orthogonal: $(1, -1, 0)$ and $(1, 0, -1)$ have inner product 1.

quiz.prose: In the proof, $\mathbf{u} \perp \mathbf{q}_1$ and $\mathbf{A}\mathbf{q}_1 = \lambda\mathbf{q}_1$. We write $\langle \mathbf{A}\mathbf{u}, \mathbf{q}_1 \rangle = \langle \mathbf{u}, \mathbf{A}\mathbf{q}_1 \rangle = \lambda\langle \mathbf{u}, \mathbf{q}_1 \rangle = 0$.
quiz.question: Which property of $\mathbf{A}$ does the first equality use?

options.why: Invertibility moves nothing across an inner product. The zero matrix is symmetric and the step still holds.
That is used to find $\mathbf{q}_1$. Moving $\mathbf{A}$ to the other slot needs $\mathbf{A}^T = \mathbf{A}$.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. What lets $\mathbf{A}$ move from one slot to the other?

byKey.real: You picked real eigenvalues. $\mathbf{N}$ has real eigenvalues and the step fails for it.

explain.text: For any real matrix, $\langle \mathbf{A}\mathbf{u}, \mathbf{q} \rangle = \langle \mathbf{u}, \mathbf{A}^T\mathbf{q} \rangle$. Symmetry turns $\mathbf{A}^T$ into $\mathbf{A}$. That is exactly what $\mathbf{N}$ lacked.

quiz.prose: $U$ is invariant under the symmetric $\mathbf{A}$, so $\mathbf{A}$ restricts to an operator $T$ on $U$.
quiz.question: Why is $T$ self-adjoint for the inner product $U$ inherits?

options.text: $\langle \mathbf{A}\mathbf{u}, \mathbf{u}' \rangle = \langle \mathbf{u}, \mathbf{A}\mathbf{u}' \rangle$ holds for all vectors, so for those in $U$
Its matrix in any basis of $U$ is symmetric
options.why: Only in an orthonormal basis of $U$. In another basis the matrix of a self-adjoint map can be non-symmetric.
The dimension sets up the induction. It says nothing about adjoints.
Real eigenvalues do not give self-adjointness, as $\mathbf{N}$ showed.

feedback.correct: Right. The identity holds on all of $\mathbb{R}^n$, so it holds on $U$.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Is the defining identity of self-adjointness about particular vectors?

byKey.basis: You trusted a matrix in any basis. Symmetric matrix and self-adjoint agree only in an orthonormal basis.

explain.text: Self-adjoint means $\langle T\mathbf{u}, \mathbf{u}' \rangle = \langle \mathbf{u}, T\mathbf{u}' \rangle$ for all $\mathbf{u}, \mathbf{u}'$ in $U$. That is a special case of the same identity for $\mathbf{A}$ on $\mathbb{R}^n$. Invariance makes $T$ an operator on $U$ in the first place.

quiz.prose: Three assets with every pairwise correlation $\rho = -0.6$ give eigenvalues $1 + 2\rho = -0.2$ and $1 - \rho = 1.6$ twice.
quiz.question: What does the eigenvalue $-0.2$ say?

options.text: No such correlation matrix exists: the market mode would have negative variance
The market mode is a perfect hedge with variance 0
options.why: Variance 0 happens at $\rho = -0.5$. At $-0.6$ it would be $-0.2 \times \tfrac13 < 0$.

options.text: Nothing: eigenvalues of a symmetric matrix may have any sign
options.why: Any symmetric matrix, yes; a correlation matrix is a covariance, and needs every eigenvalue at least 0.
Order is not the issue; the sign is.

feedback.correct: Right. A covariance matrix has $\mathbf{w}^T\mathbf{C}\mathbf{w} \ge 0$ for every $\mathbf{w}$.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Compute the variance of $\tfrac13(1, 1, 1)$ with this matrix.

byKey.fine: You allowed a negative eigenvalue. For a correlation matrix it is a portfolio with negative variance.

explain.text: $\mathbf{w} = \tfrac13(1, 1, 1)$ would have variance $-0.2 \times \tfrac13 < 0$. So three assets cannot all have correlation $-0.6$ with each other. The boundary is $\rho = -0.5$, where the smallest eigenvalue is 0.

quiz.prose: At $\rho = -0.5$ the equicorrelated $3 \times 3$ matrix has eigenvalues $1 + 2\rho$ and $1 - \rho$ twice.
quiz.question: What is the variance of $\mathbf{w} = \tfrac13(1, 1, 1)$ at $\rho = -0.5$?

feedback.correct: Right. $\mathbf{w}$ is on the market mode, whose eigenvalue $1 + 2(-0.5)$ is 0.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Which eigenvalue goes with $(1, 1, 1)$?

byKey.other: You used $(1 - \rho)\|\mathbf{w}\|^2 = 1.5 \times \tfrac13$. The market mode's eigenvalue is $1 + 2\rho$.
byKey.one: $1.5 = 1 - \rho$ is the other eigenvalue. $(1, 1, 1)$ goes with $1 + 2\rho$.

explain.text: $\mathbf{w}$ lies along $(1, 1, 1)$, with eigenvalue $1 + 2(-0.5) = 0$. So its variance is $0 \times \tfrac13 = 0$: the three assets cancel exactly. This is the boundary case of a valid correlation matrix.

options.why: A diagonal matrix is the easiest case; its eigenvectors are the standard basis.
Equal columns are dependent, so that $\mathbf{Q}$ is not orthogonal.

feedback.correct: Right. The standard basis is an orthonormal eigenbasis of a diagonal matrix.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. What are the eigenvectors of a diagonal matrix?

explain.text: $\mathbf{D}\mathbf{e}_k = d_k\mathbf{e}_k$, so the standard basis is an orthonormal eigenbasis. Then $\mathbf{Q} = \mathbf{I}$ and $\boldsymbol{\Lambda} = \mathbf{D}$. A $1 \times 1$ matrix is the same edge case, the base of the induction.
